stages.name: International competitiveness
stages.title: International competitiveness
stages.sub: What makes a country's firms competitive abroad, and what follows from having it or lacking it.

steps.q: A UK car and a German car are almost identical, but the UK one is cheaper to buy abroad. Which is a buyer in France more likely to choose?
steps.right: The UK car, because it costs less
steps.wrong: The German car, because it costs less
steps.hint: Think about which price the French buyer actually pays for each car.
steps.pre: So comparing how cheap one country's exports are against another's is a measure called

steps.q: Two phone makers charge the same price, but one phone has a better camera and longer battery life. Which will most buyers pick, even at an equal price?
steps.right: The one with the better features
steps.wrong: The one with the weaker features
steps.hint: If price does not decide it, what else about the product does?
steps.pre: So better technology, quality and design are a factor called

steps.q: One country requires firms to complete months of paperwork before they can export; another makes it quick and simple. Which country's firms can sell abroad more easily?
steps.hint: Which set of firms loses less time and money just getting to the point of selling?
steps.pre: So the rules and environment government sets for business are a factor called

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 3 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: A country's exports are cheap, well-made and produced under helpful regulation, so foreign buyers and firms increasingly choose it over rivals. What is likely to happen to its export sales, and to foreign firms wanting to invest and produce there?
steps.right: Both exports and inward investment rise
steps.wrong: Both exports and inward investment fall
steps.hint: If a country is an attractive place to sell to and to sell from, why would investors avoid it?

steps.q: Now imagine the opposite: a country's firms are expensive, low quality and slowed down by regulation, so both locals and foreigners buy imports instead of its exports. What happens to jobs in its export industries, and to how much it earns from selling abroad compared to what it spends on imports?
steps.right: Jobs are lost and it earns less than it spends on imports
steps.wrong: Jobs are gained and it earns more than it spends on imports
steps.hint: If exports are weak while imports are strong, does the country sell more or less abroad than it buys in?
